author: Vernon Fueston
title: English Learner campers present gift to Ward - NewsBreak
text:
By Vernon Fueston ,
5 hours ago
About three-dozen English language students presented a gift to Edenton-Chowan Schools Superintendent Tammi Ward.
The students, most of whom are not native English speakers, created a wall hanging of self portraits that they created in their English Learner Summer Camp. Each student made a self-portrait on the front surface of a paper plate. The class next assembled the plates into a wall hanging. They presented Ward her gift during a ceremony at Shepard-Pruden Memorial Library on Monday, June 29.
Ward praised the students’ work and asked where they thought the wall hanging should be displayed so others could see it.
“This is very, very special,” Ward told the students.
She said the school system would look for a place to hang it, possibly at the ECPS Professional Development Center, and would try to include a sign acknowledging this year’s camp.
Lucy McKellar is a English language tutor at White Oak Elementary. She said the students, who all attend either White Oak or D.F. Walker elementary schools, ranged in age from kindergarten to fifth-grade. For all of them, English is not their primary language, as they came to the United States from Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala and some Arabic speaking countries.
McKellar said the terminology for the program has changed over the years. What used to be called English as a Second Language, or ESL, was quietly changed to a new term, English Learner to remove any possible stigma. But she said the mission of the English Learner program has remained the same: to help students develop their English language skills.
“My main goal is for them to have a place where they feel that they belong,” McKellar said.
She said the camp gave students a chance to continue learning, build friendships and practice speaking, reading, writing and listening skills during the summer.
McKellar said the students have a lot more on their plate than learning a langage. They also have to acclimate to a new culture, one that can be mystifying or even potentially humiliating if their lack of familiarity makes them look “ignorant” to others. she said. McKellar spoke of one student who asked why Americans sometimes wore plastic, referring to rain jackets. In the student’s native country, the dry climate and lower standard of living made raincoats an expensive and seldom-used luxury.
McKellar said the camp offered themed activities structured around food and books. Students talked about menu items they may have never heard of, like pancakes, s’mores and tacos. They even made smores in solar ovens built from pizza boxes.
The wall hanging was designed to help students see that they belong in their schools. McKellar said she wanted them to be able to walk into a school building, see their work and say, “There’s a piece of me here.”
McKellar credited fellow ESL tutor Rosalita Muro, who works with students at D.F. Walker, the middle school and high school, with leading the art project. She also thanked ECPS staff, school principals and teachers Heather Copeland and Holland Dufresne for helping make the camp possible.
Students also received library cards, which McKellar said had been one of her dreams for the program. She said the cards give children a place to read, work on projects and continue learning after camp ends.

She said the school system would look for a place to hang it, possibly at the ECPS Professional Development Center, and would try to include a sign acknowledging this year’s camp. She said the camp gave students a chance to continue learning, build friendships and practice speaking, reading, writing and listening skills during the summer. In the student’s native country, the dry climate and lower standard of living made raincoats an expensive and seldom-used luxury.
